title: CI in the Era of AI: From Unit Tests to Stochastic Evals — Nathan Sobo, Zed

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is testing methodology for AI systems—stochastic evals, deterministic tests, and build watermarks—rather than the coding agent product itself. Zed is an AI-enabled code editor, placing it in coding assistants within the developer platforms vertical. The talk covers development and testing of AI features within an existing product's CI pipeline. summary: Nathan Sobo presents Zed's approach to testing AI-powered features in their Rust-based IDE. Zed's engineering culture is deeply empirical: they have tens of thousands of tests, use a deterministic simulated scheduler for concurrency testing with 50+ random interleavings, and pride themselves on zero flaky builds. When LLMs were introduced for Agentic Editing, this determinism broke down—one token change produces completely different output. Their first eval was a data-driven, SWE-bench-style input/output test. They evolved it into a programmatic eval where conversations are functions and assertions check agent behavior. A key insight emerged: many stochastic failures actually mask deterministic algorithmic problems. For example, a poorly-implemented grep tool was improved using tree-sitter to expand matches to syntactic boundaries, driven by a stochastic test. They encountered numerous challenges with streaming edits: tool calls don't stream well, so they switched to old-text/new-text blocks. This introduced parsing challenges—arbitrary chunking, XML tag mismatches (reduced from 40% to 5% via prompt engineering, with robustness for the remainder), empty old-text tags, indentation flattening (solved via indent-delta normalization), and escaping issues (especially with Gemini). Many of these were ultimately driven back to deterministic tests. They run evals 200 times and set watermarks requiring 100% pass rates. Sobo describes a three-stage process: start with a zoomed-out eval, zoom into a focused stochastic unit test that still interacts with the model, then drive that further into a traditional deterministic test. Importantly, they haven't needed special external eval frameworks—just their existing test suite and traditional software engineering skills, now combined with a statistical approach. Sobo notes Zed is open source under GPL and invites contributions, sharing that Claude 4 models finally enable efficient agentic Rust development.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Deterministic testing is foundational to Zed's quality, but LLMs fundamentally break determinism—one token change yields completely different output
Many seemingly stochastic failures actually mask deterministic algorithmic problems that can be isolated and fixed with traditional tests
A three-stage process works well: zoomed-out eval → focused stochastic unit test → traditional deterministic test
Evals can live in the existing test suite without special external tools or frameworks—traditional SE skills still apply
Evals should be programmatic with code-level assertions, not just data-driven input/output comparisons
Running evals 100-200 times with threshold-based pass rates provides statistical confidence for build gating
Streaming edits via tool calls is problematic; old-text/new-text blocks with robust parsing handle model output better
Prompt engineering reduces but cannot eliminate failure modes, so code must handle the residual robustly
Fuzzy matching and indentation normalization are critical bridges between imperfect LLM output and correct code edits
Traditional software engineering rigor combined with a statistical mindset embracing bounded non-determinism is the overarching lesson

sections.title: Introduction to Zed and Testing Culture
sections.summary: Sobo introduces Zed as an AI-enabled code editor built from scratch in Rust, engineered like a video game for 120fps. He describes Zed's hardcore empirical testing approach, including a simulated scheduler for deterministic concurrency testing with 50+ random interleavings. He notes that without tests, Zed would crash every 8 seconds.

sections.title: From Determinism to Stochastic Evals
sections.summary: Sobo explains how LLMs break deterministic testing since changing one input token produces completely different output. He describes evolving from data-driven ML-style evals to programmatic evals with code assertions, and shares how a stochastic eval drove out a deterministic fix using tree-sitter to expand grep tool matches to syntactic boundaries.

sections.title: Streaming Edits and Parsing Challenges
sections.summary: Sobo covers the switch from tool calls to old-text/new-text blocks for streaming edits. He describes deterministic tests for parser robustness with arbitrary chunking, fuzzy matching for approximate matches, and streaming diff logic. He shares the approach of running evals 200 times with a 100% pass watermark.

sections.title: LLM Output Edge Cases and Fixes
sections.summary: Sobo details specific LLM output problems and solutions: empty old-text tags (prompt fix + robustness), XML tag mismatches (reduced from 40% to 5% via prompts, robustness for remainder), indentation flattening (indent-delta normalization), and escaping issues especially with Gemini (prompt fix). He emphasizes rigorous testing remains fundamental, combining traditional SE techniques with statistical threshold-based approaches.

sections.title: Conclusion: Three-Stage Process and Open Source Invitation
sections.summary: Sobo describes the discovered three-stage process: start with a zoomed-out eval, zoom into a focused stochastic unit test still interacting with the model, then drive further to a traditional deterministic test. He notes they haven't needed special external eval frameworks—just their existing test suite and traditional software engineering skills combined with empirical iteration. He highlights Zed is open source under GPL, invites contributions, and shares that Claude 4 models finally enable efficient agentic Rust development.

demonstrations: Concurrency test with simulated scheduler running 50 iterations of random interleavings with replay capability
Programmatic eval where conversation is a function with code assertions about agent behavior
Deterministic test using tree-sitter to expand grep matches to syntactic boundaries

Streaming diff logic comparing emitted new text against old text dynamically

limitations: Full determinism is impossible with frontier LLMs due to token-level sensitivity
Prompt engineering reduces but cannot eliminate failure modes like XML tag mismatch (5% residual)
Escaping behavior issues, especially with Gemini, were addressed only via prompt fixes without deeper detection
Stochastic non-determinism is bounded but never fully eliminable
